title: Anatomy of a movie market
description_html:
Before an independent movie makes it to a streaming platform or a theater near you, it first needs to survive an artistic and economic gauntlet. And even for those movies that make it into elite film festivals like Sundance – it can take everything from performance stunts to corporate spycraft to seal the deal. Today on the show, we follow the ‘King of Sundance’ as he and his team try to sell their slate of movies to distributors like Netflix and Sony and Apple. We hear the behind the scenes stories about how films like Little Miss Sunshine, Napoleon Dynamite and Precious got sold. And we learn the strategies that might make the difference in whether or not a film makes it onto screens around the world.

cues.t: This is Planet Money from NPR.
The other night, I was sitting on my couch, scrolling through all the streaming movies on offer like you do, trying to decide between some new indie comedy and a broody documentary.

And then I started thinking about the actual selection available to me because I recently got a glimpse into the hidden market behind that menu, the negotiations and strategy that determine which movies make it to a screen near you.
And I learned the story of how any one film gets plucked from obscurity can be just as entertaining as the movies themselves.
It began one cold, bright January morning in a movie theater parking lot in Park City, Utah.
I'd arrived just before the start of the 2026 Sundance Film Festival to meet up with a guy named John Sloss.
Has anybody ever called you Mr. Sundance?
[LAUGHS] I've been-- yeah, the King of Sundance.
Yeah, in 2006, I think I was on page A1 of The New York Times.
And I think that article referred to me as the King of Sundance--
OK.
--which is not a title people want these days.
Kings are out of fashion.
That's true.
There are parades against that sort of thing these days.
Exactly.
John is the founder of a company called Cinetic Media, which does all sorts of things in the world of independent movies, from fundraising to PR.
But the thing that John is most known for is his work as a sales agent for films.
John's job is to turn unique pieces of cinematic art into saleable commodities.

Over the next week or so, his mission will be to get a handful of buyers representing some of the biggest companies in entertainment to see the films in his slate and convince them to make a series of multimillion dollar bets.
John's partner in this endeavor, the sort of hand of the king, is actually his nephew, Eric Sloss.
The three of us are standing in front of a huge crowd of people, lining up for the first screening of the festival.
It's for a documentary about mountaineering called The Last First, Winter K2.
But Eric has his eyes peeled for a very particular handful of people.
The real audience for our purposes at this festival, specifically, is very small, and that is about 10 people who can buy a documentary at the level that we're interested in.
It's Netflix, Apple, Amazon-- places like that.
Do you get, like, butterflies before the festival opens?
Yeah, it's like the minutes before the big game.
This is sort of the only Wild West environment left in the entertainment industry, and that is inherently exciting.
One big part of John and Eric's job is to push for their films to play at the best possible time and venue.
For this documentary, they had managed to get a theater with one of the bigger screens and better sound systems in Park City, which is perfect for an epic outdoor film.
But getting the first time slot of the whole festival, Eric says that was a bit of a tough draw.
And we're really nervous that because it's the first screening of the festival, that people wouldn't be in town.
Are you, like, looking around and just double-checking that the people you wanted to see in the room are here?
We are tracking buyers as they're coming in.
Do you know all the buyers by face?
More or less.
We actually have trading cards that we've created.
[LAUGHS] OK, have we got most of them?
Have we collected them all?
I think we've done a pretty good job here.
We've had people from Apple, Amazon, Disney.
Just then, John waves to a guy with salt and pepper hair and thick, black-framed glasses.
Eugene!
The first screening.
Oh, my god.
Thanks, buddy boy.
Eugene Hernandez is the head of the Sundance Film Festival.
Every year, he and his team winnow down thousands of submissions to just around 100.
But making it into the festival does not guarantee that a film will actually sell.
How are we feeling about the market this year?
I'm always hopeful on the first day.
It's always hard to predict exactly how the market will respond.
I see buyers walking up right now.
Exciting.
Head of acquisitions for Sony Classics right there.
All right.
So, you know, Dylan's got to write a check, and then the movie gets-- is out there.

Before this moment, I don't think I'd fully realized exactly how small and personal the entertainment industry can be, this idea that the commercial fate of any given film might ultimately come down to the tastes and calculations of a tiny handful of decision-makers.
Welcome, welcome, folks.
Plenty of seats available closer to the middle, as close to the middle as you can get. Thank you.
We take our seats near the front of the theater.
The house lights start to dim, the crowd begins to hush, and the first light of the festival illuminates the screen.

John and Eric sneak glances around the theater because the way this first ever audience reacts could make the difference between an all-night bidding war or being relegated to the dustbin of Sundance history.
Hello, and welcome to Planet Money.
I'm Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi.
In the world of independent film, getting your movie into a place like Sundance might seem like making it to the top of the filmmaking mountain.
But it turns out that, at least commercially speaking, getting accepted is a little more like getting to base camp.
To get to the summit, the realm of movie theaters and streaming platforms, you actually need to sell that movie to someone who can put it onto screens around the world.
Today on the show, the anatomy of a movie market.
We follow a pair of seasoned sales agents through Sundance, through the gauntlet of exclusive parties, stunt performances, corporate spycraft, and backroom deals.
We learn how this festival transformed the industry and get a peek into the messy business of turning cinematic art into cold, hard cash.
Now, movies can make their way to screens around the world in different ways.
There is, of course, the big blockbuster fare, the Marvel and Pixar movies produced by Hollywood studios.
There are things like Netflix movies made by Netflix to stream on their own platform.
And then there are what we call the independent movies, the scrappier, lower budget films that often show up in places like the Oscars stage.
Those are the movies that are mostly bought and sold at film festivals like Sundance.
Sales agent John Sloss, sometimes called the King of Sundance, first started going to the festival back in the mid 1980s.
It had been founded by movie star Robert Redford as a place to celebrate independent filmmaking and protect it from the market forces of Hollywood.
But John says the breakout success of one movie in particular quickly transformed how the industry saw the festival.
The inflection point at Sundance was 1989, when Soderbergh brought Sex, Lies, and Videotape.
That changed everything.
Steven Soderbergh's Sex, Lies, and Videotape was this low-budget feature film that took the festival by storm and eventually went on to gross over $36 million.
And John says that kind of profit margin demonstrated to the whole Hollywood ecosystem that independent arthouse films could compete with studio blockbusters.
After that, Hollywood studios started opening their own specialty divisions dedicated to acquiring and producing independent films.
And Sundance became one of the biggest markets for all those new indies, teeming with movie stars, up-and-coming directors, corporate buyers, and sales agents like John.

Now, John says, when it comes to the art of actually selling an indie film, you can think of it as sort of a delicate two-step dance, because at the beginning, the most important thing is making sure that potential Hollywood power brokers actually see your movie in the most favorable screening context possible.
But the second phase, where you begin actually hammering out the details, that can require some hard-line negotiating.
This has always been the inherent conflict because you need to be ingratiating to distributors before you screen the film to get them to come to your film.
And then once they do, you need to turn into an SOB and optimize the deal.
Yeah.
And so it's like a Jekyll and Hyde situation.
John says the way he's tried to handle that tension within his company is to make a sort of division of emotional labor.
I'm always more comfortable as the bad cop.
I love negotiating.
And I always try to get ingratiating people out in front of me to try and get the distributors to it, so that it doesn't seem too odd that I would switch on a dime.
Yeah.
But that's a big part of it, that kind of transition.
But the way you tango with potential buyers depends on the kind of movie you're trying to sell.
I asked John to walk me through some of the biggest deals he's made in his 40 years at the festival and what he's learned.
First, John told me, you might think his job might be to talk up the movie he's selling as loudly as possible, but John says there is a real danger in building up too much buzz.
The roads of Sundance past are littered with the bodies of films that got overhyped.
The hot film coming into Sundance is never the hot film going out of Sundance.

And so, if you have a film that you think can be successful, it may seem counterintuitive, but the best instinct there is to downplay it, to create the lowest expectations possible while getting all the necessary people in the theater.
John says one of the best examples of this strategy came back in 2003.
His company, Cinetic, came across a low-budget indie feature from a couple of first-time filmmakers ahead of the festival.
That was a film that sort of came in over the transom.
It was, like, a $200,000 film that was made by a bunch of Mormon kids in Preston, Idaho.
And we flipped out over it.
John and his colleagues signed the filmmakers onto their sales slate for the next Sundance, but he says they decided that the best strategy in this case would be to keep that information a secret.

They were essentially betting that audiences would find it just as charming as they did and that the organic momentum of people talking about this sleeper gem would help the odds of selling it more than any direct pitch to buyers.
That movie, by the way--
[AUDIO PLAYBACK]
What are you drawing?
A liger.
What's a liger?
--was a kind of bizarre comedy by the name of Napoleon Dynamite.
It's pretty much my favorite animal.
It's like a lion and a tiger mixed, bred for its skills and magic.
The discovery of Napoleon Dynamite was atomic within that film festival.
Yeah.
And that's when the market really, you know, matured.
Napoleon Dynamite was shot for around $200,000.
They sold it for about $5 million.
And John says what happened after it hit theaters helps illustrate why studios and distributors were so interested in indie films.
It grossed $44 million, but with DVD sales, the revenue was, I think, like, $170 million on a $200,000 film.
Now, usually, John says, the job of a sales agent is basically to chase after the buyers and drum up demand.
But he says there are some exceptions to that.
If you're lucky enough to have a popular film, as far as I'm concerned, that's when things flip.
That's when we're no longer selling.

That's when the distributors now have to sell the filmmakers on why they should commit their baby, the thing they've birthed for 18 months, to someone who hasn't had anything to do with it, and not only that, has 10 other films to release after it.
John points to one film a few years after Napoleon Dynamite as a quintessential case study.
It was a quirky family road trip movie called Little Miss Sunshine.
[AUDIO PLAYBACK]
OK, Little Miss Sunshine is a beauty contest for everyone in Albuquerque, but you have to be six or seven, and you have to be a girl.
Remember when Olive was here last month, she was runner-up in the regional Little Miss Sunshine?
Now she has a place in the state contest in Redondo--
[SQUEALING]
John and his colleagues thought they had a crowd-pleaser on their hands, but instead of trying to fly under the radar, they leaned a little bit into the hype.
They convinced the Sundance programmers to schedule their premiere on the first Friday night of the festival in the biggest, grandest theater in town.
Which is a high school auditorium, but it's a weirdly hot place to screen a movie, meaning that films play well there.
Still, as the lights dimmed, John says nobody really had any idea how the movie would land with an actual audience.
But, he says, it became clear almost immediately.
People were losing it.
It was like they piped nitrous oxide into the theater.
And about 15 minutes into the film, I said to my assistant, we got to get out of here, or we're going to be dead.
When this-- when the lights came up, we're going to-- you know, they're going to descend on us.
Now, John says, this was obviously the dream scenario, but he knew he still needed to play it right.
And so in the middle of the screening, he whispers to the filmmakers.
I said, look, go to where the party is, and I'm going to disappear.
John and his assistant make a strategic exit from the theater.
My assistant and I went out on the side door, and we thought we were going to the parking lot.
We ended up in the middle of the football field at the high school with, like, two feet of snow.
And we had to climb over this fence.
My assistant ended up cutting his hand and everything.
And we just disappeared.
We went to the interstate, and we went to this place, Ruby Tuesdays, which is famous for their bottomless salad bar.
And we sat there.
And my phone completely exploded, and I didn't answer a single call.
And I had said to the filmmakers, when the buyers are going insane, and they're looking for me, and they come to the party, just say, I don't know where Sloss is.
I think he's off doing his thing.
An aloof air of mystery.
Yes, and we did that for about three hours.
And then we decided to prioritize the buyers and have them come by.
You see, every year, John and his colleagues at Cinetic rent the same Lincoln Log chalet just outside of town.
And that is where he and his team and the Little Miss Sunshine directors retreat in order to begin the next part of the proceeding, the coveted bidding war.
This is when each of the interested buyers put together their best pitches.
And this isn't just about offering the most money.
Each buyer wants to convince the filmmakers and agents that they would be best positioned to bring the film to the wider world.
They'll tell you the comparable films they've done.
They'll tell you how much commitment they're going to make.
You try to say, how many theaters will you commit to?
At the same time, you're negotiating the deal.
John says some filmmakers might prefer to go to a company that can promise a well-funded Oscars campaign.
If it's a film about a social issue, maybe they'll care most that the film is screened in particular communities or that it sparks a broader policy conversation.
But if it's a first-time director, picking the right distributor is also largely about the long game because--
There's a good chance that the person you choose is going to be the company that that filmmaker stays in business with, even beyond this film.
You might be arranging a marriage.
Yeah, in a certain way.
You're a yenta.

In the case of Little Miss Sunshine, John says the filmmakers were eventually swayed by one company's plan to play the film way beyond the arthouse theater circuit to support an awards campaign and to pay over $10 million.
And that was a film where we stayed up all night and closed it for a record at that point in the morning.
So that is how an almost universally well-received movie can end up making it through the sales gauntlet.
But convincing anyone to buy a film can also be an extremely uphill battle.

John says, if you want to really understand how much strategy and labor and luck can go into selling a movie and getting it to a wider audience, there's perhaps no better example than the story of the film Precious.
It's a pretty hardcore movie about this overweight African-American girl who just gets abused by everyone.
[AUDIO PLAYBACK]
Nobody loved me.
People do love you, Precious.
Your baby loves you.
I love you.
John says he first heard about Precious in the lead-up to Sundance in January of 2009.
It was from a relatively green director named Lee Daniels.
We saw the film.
We realized its quality.
But you've got to ask yourself, who's the audience for this film?
Because part of what you're doing when you're selling is making the case to a distributor who the audience is and how big it is.
John tells Lee that he thinks the film is beautiful and that he would like to help him sell it, but he worries the themes of physical and sexual abuse may make it a difficult sell.
And I said to Lee Daniels, I said, I've been involved in a film like this before.
We did a film called Slam, which was a big phenomenon at Sundance, and we sold it to Lionsgate.
And then we took the film directly to the Magic Johnson theaters around Compton and did a test screening for an African-American audience, and the film screened abysmally.
John says Slam was kind of a cautionary tale for buyers.
It revealed that sometimes a film will be a hit with the largely white, relatively affluent audiences at Sundance, but fall flat with audiences of color, or vice versa.
Sometimes a film will fall into some uncanny valley between them all.
And John worried Precious might be at risk of doing just that.
And Lee Daniels, to his credit, said, you're wrong.
And here's what I'm going to do.
I'm going to book a test screening at the Magic Johnson theater on 125th Street in Harlem.
Everyone in that audience will be a person of color.
You come and sit in the audience, and you will see that this film plays completely different for a Black audience than it does for the audience at Sundance.
Yeah.
And we did a test screening, you know, where you have scores and things like that, because that's also a tool that you can use.
And the film played, and people were falling out of their chairs, laughing.
And it scored huge.

And so, we went to Sundance with the test results, so that when we got this word from distributors that they loved it, but they wouldn't know how-- a white audience wouldn't go see it or a Black audience wouldn't go see it, and then we could show them the results of this test that a Black audience would love this movie.
And that would be their sort of downside protection.
So John decides to rep the film for sale at the festival.
They bring it to Sundance and do everything they can to get the big buyers into the room to see it.
So we screened the film at that big theater, and Harvey Weinstein comes up to me and says, this is a brilliant movie, but I have no idea how to market it.
I'm like, oh, we're screwed.
But John says he also got word that someone with connections to Tyler Perry had loved the film and thought they should screen it for Tyler as soon as possible.
The only problem?
Tyler Perry is on his way to Washington for the Obama inauguration.
So we got a print to Washington, DC.
Tyler Perry watched it and flipped out and just said, what can I possibly do to help with this?
And Lee Daniels, being the canny guy that he is--
Yeah.
--said, show it to Oprah. So--
Wow.
--we arranged to get the film to Oprah.
But by the last couple days of Sundance, John and Lee still haven't heard whether Oprah had seen the film or whether she liked it.
And while the film was doing OK at the festival-- audiences seemed generally warm and it had gotten some positive reviews-- there still weren't any tangible bites when it came to actually selling it.
And then the awards night comes at Sundance.
So this is, like, right at the end.
And we're sitting there at the awards ceremony, and Lee Daniels' cell phone rings in the audience.
And he doesn't recognize the number.
And for some reason, he answered the phone anyway.
And it was Oprah.
And Oprah says, your film split me wide open.
I will do anything to help you.
And then the film goes on to win both the Audience Award and the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance.
So it's anointed.
John says after the festival, they sold the film to Lionsgate for about $5 million.
And the film ended up grossing over $50 million.
It played to both Black and white audiences.
But it could have very easily have just gone away if this series of events hadn't happened.
Yeah.
You have to, you know-- you have to lean into your luck or realize things that you didn't anticipate and pivot.

John says the story of Precious is the perfect illustration of the highly contingent way that movies are often bought and sold and all the surprising deal-making that can ultimately make the difference between a movie that stays trapped in the festival circuit forever and one that breaks out onto screens across the country.
Now, in the years since Precious, the movie business has been through some pretty major twists and turns itself.

It's gone from a seller's market during the so-called streaming wars, when sales agents like John could play highly competitive streamers against traditional movie distributors to get better deals, to a softer market after COVID emptied out movie theaters and a succession of major mergers led to belt tightening in Hollywood.

And so that is the stage for the drama about to unfold on the snowy streets of Park City at this year's Sundance, where John and Eric will try to find the right buyers for their portfolio of precious filmic art.
That's coming up after the break.
OK, so that was our time traveling journey through some of the biggest deals of Sundance's past.
Now we return to this year's festival to see up close what it's like to try to sway film buyers today.
We began our story, you'll recall, at the first screening of the festival, a mountaineering documentary called The Last First, Winter K2, that John and Eric Sloss are selling.
After the screening, I catch up with Eric to hear about what the next week will look like.
The next week is moments of punctuated action with long waits in between.
There's a little, like, purgatorial quality to some of it.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah, there's a lot of sitting around and waiting for people to call.
The opening of the festival, he says, is like the starting pistol for a race that'll play out over the next five or so days.

Now, a lot of the strategy and competition that will determine their success or failure, John explains, actually begins way before the festival, because in addition to pitching films and fielding offers from buyers, John's job is to select films with potential out of over 1,000 they watch every year, and then to convince filmmakers to let his company represent the movie.

John says, in recent years, that part of the work has gotten a lot harder, because while Cinetic started out as one of the first big movers in this market, over the past decade or two, a new group of competitors have been encroaching into their territory.
The big Hollywood talent agencies, like William Morris Endeavor or Creative Artists Agency, represent actors and writers and directors.

They were already putting together the deals to get various projects off the ground, and so, John says, they started proposing more and more that when it came time to sell that film, they should be the ones handling that negotiation, too.
So, many of the films John and Eric might have otherwise signed onto their sales slate were already spoken for.
And it really cut into our business, which is part of the reason, for many years, we really had a hard time getting scripted films.
Yeah.
You know?
Because we have to survive, we sort of pivoted toward documentaries and worked hard to sort of increase the value of documentaries in the marketplace.
Out of the 10 movies Cinetic is representing at Sundance this year, six of them are documentaries.
So that is the competition John and Eric face in the lead-up to the festival.

But once they actually get there, they not only want to get the right buyers in the room, but they also want to fill the room with sympathetic audience members, maybe get a few film critics or topical influencers to get the buzzball rolling and hopefully nudge those buyers toward an offer.
I like to call this strategy "controlling the narrative," a.k.a. inception.

This has always been part of the Sundance sales game, but John says that trying to get the right mixture of reviews at just the right time has become much more difficult, as things like Letterboxd and X have democratized the conversation over any given movie.
Yeah, and the first person who writes about a film can be the controlling voice.
And beyond trying to control the narrative around their films, John and Eric need to keep tabs on the competition at Sundance, on how buyers are reacting to all the movies they are not representing.
And some of what they're doing basically boils down to good old-fashioned spycraft.
I mean, we have 14 people here.
They're hardwired into the community.
You just sort of send them out, and some of them go to the screenings and see who's congregating afterwards.
Yeah, it's like a full intelligence [LAUGHS] kind of operation.
I like to call this one "behind frenemy lines," because sometimes a bidding war will break out for another company's movie, and that could potentially impact John and Eric's sales prospects.
The buyers at this festival, the big theatrical distributors and streaming companies, they only have so much cash to spend on new acquisitions.

So a shiny, bright, new object that everybody wants could tie up a lot of money and attention, at least until the winning buyer emerges, and all the runners-up are freed up again to chase other possible movies.
Now, beyond these kinds of information management and intelligence gathering, Eric tells me they sometimes resort to old-fashioned showmanship.
They'll put on a kind of stunt event to hopefully woo buyers.
This year, for example, one of the documentaries on Cinetic Slate is a movie called The Disciple, which tells the story of a clandestinely recorded Wu-Tang Clan album with only one copy in the world.
In order to build hype for that film, Eric decided to put together an exclusive listening party at a fancy chalet outside of town.
And that is where I met him a couple days into the festival.
We are down valley from Park City at the chairman of the board of the Sundance Film Festival's house.
And what are we here for?
We are here to listen to, for the first time, five full songs from the Wu-Tang Clan album Once Upon a Time in Shaolin.
What do you call this type of move?
Sundance theater.
This is some classic Sundance theater.
Yeah, it's its own genre.
Included in this genre, the premiere of the documentary, Exit Through the Gift Shop, about the street artist Banksy.

That coincided with the mysterious appearance of several new pieces of Banksy's art around Park City, or the time influential critics and festival goers were invited to a midnight secret screening with no idea what they were about to see, only to be surprised with the world premiere of Jordan Peele's Get Out.
As for this year's stunt, Eric is betting that an exclusive listening party for an album that has never been publicly released will play on his potential buyers' FOMO.
And I assume I can record, get a snippet of the album, all that?
There is a strict no-record policy.
When the album starts, everybody will be required to put their phones in Yonder pouches, and they'll be secured until after the album is finished.
What do you hope happens in there?
The only goal here is for people to enjoy the experience of watching this.
We don't need, like, the checkbooks to start coming out mid-party?
If they want to bring them out, that's fine.
[LAUGHS] The bidding war could start on the dance floor.
We'll set up a table, and they can form an orderly queue.
Eric and I head inside.

And for those of you curious about what I heard beyond the doors of that stately home, I can only say that much like Odysseus tied to the mast of his ship as it passed the Isle of the Sirens, there are some songs that simply cannot be captured by human language.
In any event, over the next few days, I only managed to catch glimpses of John and Eric here and there, as they run between various screenings and parties.
Finally, on Monday night, I find myself at the grand finale of their sales gauntlet, the extremely popular Cinetic party that celebrates the close of the first weekend of the festival.
When I arrived, there are dozens and dozens of people lined up outside in the 27 degree cold.
Some had been waiting for over an hour.
Inside, I find Eric in a packed part of the bar.
We're at High West Saloon for what I think is probably one of the oldest parties at Sundance.
Everybody's exhausted enough to come together and just let loose, but also a gathering where lots of deals end up taking place.
How do deals end up happening at a party?
Look, when you're trapped in a room and everybody's drunk, it's easy to have these conversations.
This is how movies really get sold over, like, an old fashioned in a old-timey, pickax-themed mining tavern.
And like I said, it's the Wild West.
What's your drink of choice?
Unfortunately, I don't drink at this party.
That seems smart.
Yeah, it's good to be the only one.

Yes. [LAUGHS] Let's call this strategy "loose lips grease deals." And while I don't actually happen to spy any deals going down amidst the revelry, I do get a call two days later from Eric and John inviting me to join them at their inner sanctum, the Cinetic Lincoln Log mansion, where so many sales have been closed over the years.
They pick me up in a strip mall parking lot and whisk me into the mountains.
John, where are we right now?
We are at the condo in Deer Valley that we have rented for the last 24 or 25 years.
Some of the biggest and most consequential deals in the history of the Sundance Film Festival have been consummated where you are sitting.
It's kind of like a holy space.
It's a holy space.
John points to the place in the room where reps from some of the biggest streamers and studios in the world come to make their appeals.
They'll come in and they'll sit, and the filmmakers will sit.
And we'll do negotiating.
Yeah, it's where commerce happens.
[LAUGHS] It's where art becomes commerce.
Commerce, yes.
Then John starts filling me in on what happened after that first screening of the festival.
Apparently, the head of documentary at one of the big streamers reached out to John and Eric to say they were interested.
But in this era of more limited budgets and corporate bureaucracy, they couldn't actually start negotiating until they had approval from their boss.
So John and the rest of the company sprang into action, setting up a private screening in the basement theater of the Lincoln Log chalet.
Finally, the big boss arrives.
And then we started the film and made ourselves scarce.
And it could have gone either way.
You know, we knew that the head of documentaries loved the film, but if this guy didn't, an offer probably would not have materialized.
This is like what you need to get the sign-off.
In this case, yeah.
I asked John what he means about an offer materializing, and he hesitates for a moment.
I don't know when you're going to be on the air, but if you're going to be on the air tomorrow, I can't tell you this.
No, no, no.
In, like-- probably in, like, 10 months or something.
Oh, well, we just closed the first film, which is The Last First, K2 in Winter.
We closed with Apple.
It's a documentary.
Wow. That's--
You're the first to hear it.
That's huge news.
You people are the last to hear it.
You, Alexi, are the first to hear it.

segments.text: So, many of the films John and Eric might have otherwise signed onto their sales slate were already spoken for.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: And it really cut into our business, which is part of the reason, for many years, we really had a hard time getting scripted films.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: You know? Because we have to survive, we sort of pivoted toward documentaries and worked hard to sort of increase the value of documentaries in the marketplace.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Out of the 10 movies Cinetic is representing at Sundance this year, six of them are documentaries. So that is the competition John and Eric face in the lead-up to the festival. But once they actually get there, they not only want to get the right buyers in the room, but they also want to fill the room with sympathetic audience members, maybe get a few film critics or topical influencers to get the buzzball rolling and hopefully nudge those buyers toward an offer.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: I like to call this strategy "controlling the narrative," a.k.a. inception. This has always been part of the Sundance sales game, but John says that trying to get the right mixture of reviews at just the right time has become much more difficult, as things like Letterboxd and X have democratized the conversation over any given movie.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: Yeah, and the first person who writes about a film can be the controlling voice.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: And beyond trying to control the narrative around their films, John and Eric need to keep tabs on the competition at Sundance, on how buyers are reacting to all the movies they are not representing. And some of what they're doing basically boils down to good old-fashioned spycraft.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: I mean, we have 14 people here. They're hardwired into the community. You just sort of send them out, and some of them go to the screenings and see who's congregating afterwards.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Yeah, it's like a full intelligence [LAUGHS] kind of operation. I like to call this one "behind frenemy lines," because sometimes a bidding war will break out for another company's movie, and that could potentially impact John and Eric's sales prospects. The buyers at this festival, the big theatrical distributors and streaming companies, they only have so much cash to spend on new acquisitions. So a shiny, bright, new object that everybody wants could tie up a lot of money and attention, at least until the winning buyer emerges, and all the runners-up are freed up again to chase other possible movies.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Now, beyond these kinds of information management and intelligence gathering, Eric tells me they sometimes resort to old-fashioned showmanship. They'll put on a kind of stunt event to hopefully woo buyers. This year, for example, one of the documentaries on Cinetic Slate is a movie called The Disciple, which tells the story of a clandestinely recorded Wu-Tang Clan album with only one copy in the world. In order to build hype for that film, Eric decided to put together an exclusive listening party at a fancy chalet outside of town.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: And that is where I met him a couple days into the festival.

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: We are down valley from Park City at the chairman of the board of the Sundance Film Festival's house.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: And what are we here for?

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: We are here to listen to, for the first time, five full songs from the Wu-Tang Clan album Once Upon a Time in Shaolin.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: What do you call this type of move?

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: Sundance theater.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: This is some classic Sundance theater.

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: Yeah, it's its own genre.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Included in this genre, the premiere of the documentary, Exit Through the Gift Shop, about the street artist Banksy. That coincided with the mysterious appearance of several new pieces of Banksy's art around Park City, or the time influential critics and festival goers were invited to a midnight secret screening with no idea what they were about to see, only to be surprised with the world premiere of Jordan Peele's Get Out.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: As for this year's stunt, Eric is betting that an exclusive listening party for an album that has never been publicly released will play on his potential buyers' FOMO. And I assume I can record, get a snippet of the album, all that?

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: There is a strict no-record policy. When the album starts, everybody will be required to put their phones in Yonder pouches, and they'll be secured until after the album is finished.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: What do you hope happens in there?

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: The only goal here is for people to enjoy the experience of watching this.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: We don't need, like, the checkbooks to start coming out mid-party?

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: If they want to bring them out, that's fine.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: [LAUGHS] The bidding war could start on the dance floor.

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: We'll set up a table, and they can form an orderly queue.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Eric and I head inside. And for those of you curious about what I heard beyond the doors of that stately home, I can only say that much like Odysseus tied to the mast of his ship as it passed the Isle of the Sirens, there are some songs that simply cannot be captured by human language. In any event, over the next few days, I only managed to catch glimpses of John and Eric here and there, as they run between various screenings and parties.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Finally, on Monday night, I find myself at the grand finale of their sales gauntlet, the extremely popular Cinetic party that celebrates the close of the first weekend of the festival. When I arrived, there are dozens and dozens of people lined up outside in the 27 degree cold. Some had been waiting for over an hour. Inside, I find Eric in a packed part of the bar.

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: We're at High West Saloon for what I think is probably one of the oldest parties at Sundance. Everybody's exhausted enough to come together and just let loose, but also a gathering where lots of deals end up taking place.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: How do deals end up happening at a party?

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: Look, when you're trapped in a room and everybody's drunk, it's easy to have these conversations.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: This is how movies really get sold over, like, an old fashioned in a old-timey, pickax-themed mining tavern.

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: And like I said, it's the Wild West.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: What's your drink of choice?

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: Unfortunately, I don't drink at this party.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: That seems smart.

segments.speaker: Eric Sloss
segments.text: Yeah, it's good to be the only one.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Yes. [LAUGHS] Let's call this strategy "loose lips grease deals." And while I don't actually happen to spy any deals going down amidst the revelry, I do get a call two days later from Eric and John inviting me to join them at their inner sanctum, the Cinetic Lincoln Log mansion, where so many sales have been closed over the years. They pick me up in a strip mall parking lot and whisk me into the mountains.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: John, where are we right now?

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: We are at the condo in Deer Valley that we have rented for the last 24 or 25 years. Some of the biggest and most consequential deals in the history of the Sundance Film Festival have been consummated where you are sitting.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: It's kind of like a holy space.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: It's a holy space.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: John points to the place in the room where reps from some of the biggest streamers and studios in the world come to make their appeals.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: They'll come in and they'll sit, and the filmmakers will sit. And we'll do negotiating. Yeah, it's where commerce happens.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: [LAUGHS] It's where art becomes commerce.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: Commerce, yes.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Then John starts filling me in on what happened after that first screening of the festival. Apparently, the head of documentary at one of the big streamers reached out to John and Eric to say they were interested. But in this era of more limited budgets and corporate bureaucracy, they couldn't actually start negotiating until they had approval from their boss. So John and the rest of the company sprang into action, setting up a private screening in the basement theater of the Lincoln Log chalet.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Finally, the big boss arrives.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: And then we started the film and made ourselves scarce. And it could have gone either way. You know, we knew that the head of documentaries loved the film, but if this guy didn't, an offer probably would not have materialized.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: This is like what you need to get the sign-off.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: In this case, yeah.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: I asked John what he means about an offer materializing, and he hesitates for a moment.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: I don't know when you're going to be on the air, but if you're going to be on the air tomorrow, I can't tell you this.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: No, no, no. In, like-- probably in, like, 10 months or something.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: Oh, well, we just closed the first film, which is The Last First, K2 in Winter. We closed with Apple. It's a documentary.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: Wow. That's--

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: You're the first to hear it.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: That's huge news.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: You people are the last to hear it. You, Alexi, are the first to hear it.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: All right, well, this is a time capsule into the future. Congratulations. That seems like a big deal.

segments.speaker: John Sloss
segments.text: It is a big deal. And everyone's happy.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: John tells me the rest of the sales are still in flux, but that he'll keep me posted. For the time being, we have to rush out the door to make it to a screening across town. We get to the theater just in time, say our goodbyes, and I watch him disappear into the crowd. And sure enough, now, about nine months after my visit to Sundance, when I put some popcorn in the microwave, sink into the couch, and scroll through the latest streaming options on TV, I see the mountaineering documentary, The Last First, streaming on Apple, and the Wu-Tang documentary, The Disciple, which just opened on Netflix.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi
segments.text: But now, I think not just about all the artistry that went into actually making those films, but also, the deal-making that got them out into the world. And then, of course, I keep on scrolling with no end in sight, because actually choosing what to watch, that, my friends, is the hardest summit of all.

segments.speaker: Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi

Alex Goldmark is Planet Money's executive producer. Special thanks to Madison [? Murray,?] Bennett Levine, Alexandra Garcia, and Alyse Shorland. I'm Alexi Horowitz-Ghazi. This is NPR. Thanks for listening.

study.one_liner_ko: 인디 영화가 선댄스에서 어떻게 팔리는지, 세일즈 에이전트 존 슬로스와 에릭 슬로스를 따라가며 보여주는 영화 시장의 해부 이야기.
summary_ko: 선댄스 영화제에 선정되는 것은 정상이 아니라 베이스캠프에 도착한 것에 가깝다. 영화를 실제 스크린에 올리려면 넷플릭스, 애플, 소니 같은 소수의 구매자에게 팔아야 한다.
세일즈 에이전트 존 슬로스는 상영 전에는 구매자에게 살갑게 굴고, 상영 후에는 냉정한 협상가로 돌변해야 한다고 말한다. 그는 이를 '지킬 앤 하이드'에 비유하고, 자신은 '나쁜 경찰' 역할이 편하다고 한다.
과도한 기대감은 독이라서 때로는 기대치를 낮추는 편이 낫다. 「나폴레옹 다이너마이트」는 조용히 입소문을 노려 성공했고, 「리틀 미스 선샤인」은 반대로 정면으로 기세를 탔다.
「프리셔스」는 관객층이 불확실해 구매자가 꺼렸다. 감독의 테스트 상영, 타일러 페리와 오프라의 지지, 선댄스 수상이 이어지며 극적으로 팔렸고, 존은 운을 활용하고 방향을 틀 줄 알아야 한다고 정리한다.
최근에는 대형 에이전시의 잠식과 SNS 리뷰 때문에 시장이 어려워졌다. 슬로스 팀은 다큐 쪽으로 방향을 틀고, 경쟁사 동향을 정탐하고, 우탱 클랜 청음회 같은 '선댄스 시어터'와 파티로 구매자를 공략한다.
결국 올해 「The Last First」는 애플에, 「The Disciple」은 넷플릭스에 팔렸다. 화면 뒤에는 소수 결정권자를 향한 치밀한 전략과 운이 있었다.
study.summary_en: This Planet Money episode follows John and Eric Sloss, sales agents who try to sell indie films at Sundance. Getting in is just base camp. The real summit is convincing a handful of buyers at places like Netflix and Apple to write a check. John says you have to be charming before the screening and ruthless afterward. Sometimes you downplay a film, like Napoleon Dynamite, and sometimes you lean into the hype, like Little Miss Sunshine. Precious almost died until Oprah and the awards rescued it. Today the market is tougher, so they run stunts, spy on rivals and close deals at parties. In the end, both their big films got picked up.

expressions.nuance_ko: 출판·영화 업계에서 '투고 원고'처럼 예상 밖 경로로 들어온 것을 가리킨다. 약간 업계 용어 느낌이 있어 일상에서는 드물지만 아는 척하기 좋다.
examples: Honestly, our best hire came in over the transom. He just emailed us out of the blue.
The story came in over the transom, and the editor almost ignored it.
Half our best ideas come in over the transom, not from the planning meetings.

similar.example: She called me out of the blue last night.
We get a lot of unsolicited pitches.

expressions.meaning_ko: 너무 좋아서 또는 화가 나서 정신 못 차리다
expressions.nuance_ko: 구어체로 긍정·부정 둘 다 쓴다. 문맥으로 구분하며, 여기서는 '엄청 반했다'는 뜻이다. 격식 있는 자리에서는 'be thrilled'로 바꾼다.
examples: My kids flipped out when they saw the snow this morning.
My boss flipped out when she saw the typo in the slide.
We flipped out over that little ramen place near the hotel.

similar.example: Everyone went nuts over the new phone.
I totally lost it when they announced the winner.

expressions.quote: I would switch on a dime
expressions.nuance_ko: 'turn on a dime'이 원형이고 'switch'도 쓴다. 사람의 태도 급변과 조직의 민첩함을 모두 가리킨다. 긍정이면 민첩함, 부정이면 변덕스러움이다.
examples: Our manager can switch on a dime when a client pushes back.
Small teams can turn on a dime, which is their big advantage.
The weather here switches on a dime, so bring a jacket.

similar.example: He did a 180 on the budget after the meeting.
We had to pivot quickly when the supplier dropped out.

expressions.expression: be littered with the bodies of
expressions.quote: littered with the bodies of films that got overhyped
expressions.nuance_ko: 'The road to X is littered with failed Y'는 실패 사례가 많다는 경고에 쓰는 수사 패턴이다. 발표나 토론에서 인상적으로 문장을 시작할 때 좋다.
examples: The startup world is littered with the bodies of companies that scaled too fast.
The road to a perfect diet is littered with broken New Year's resolutions.
This industry is littered with the bodies of good ideas that launched at the wrong time.

similar.example: Retail is the graveyard of overconfident brands.
The history of tech is strewn with failed predictions.

expressions.quote: it may seem counterintuitive, but the best instinct there is to downplay it
expressions.nuance_ko: 'it may seem counterintuitive, but…'은 반직관적 주장을 꺼낼 때의 디스코스 마커다. 'downplay expectations'는 '기대치 관리'의 구어적 표현이다.
examples: I always downplay expectations before a big presentation, then overdeliver.
The coach downplayed their chances before the final.
It may seem counterintuitive, but admitting a weakness early builds trust.

similar.example: We need to manage expectations with the client.
She played down the injury to avoid worrying everyone.

expressions.nuance_ko: 'drum up business/support/interest'로 확장해 쓴다. 애써서 없던 관심을 만든다는 뉘앙스가 있다.
examples: We ran a free-trial week to drum up demand for the new gym.
He's trying to drum up support for the petition.
The cafe handed out samples to drum up some business.

similar.example: The teaser trailer generated a lot of buzz.
They whipped up interest with a launch party.

expressions.nuance_ko: 'That's when + 절' 패턴으로 전환점을 짚는다. 힘의 균형이 바뀌는 순간을 말할 때 협상 이야기에 자주 쓴다.
examples: When you have two job offers, that's when things flip and you're the one negotiating.
Once the product sells out, that's when things flip and customers wait for you.
The moment the landlord needs a tenant, that's when things flip.

similar.example: Then the tables turned, and they were begging us to stay.
That's the tipping point where we gain leverage.

expressions.quote: trying to fly under the radar
expressions.nuance_ko: 주목을 피하는 게 의도일 수도 있고 그냥 덜 알려진 상태일 수도 있다. 문장에서 긍정·부정 모두 가능하다.
examples: The small bakery flew under the radar until a food blogger found it.
I'd rather fly under the radar at the office party and leave early.
That stock has been flying under the radar for years.

similar.example: He kept a low profile after the merger news.
The change went unnoticed for months.

expressions.quote: you have to lean into your luck
expressions.nuance_ko: 피하지 않고 오히려 그 특성이나 흐름을 강점으로 쓴다는 뜻이다. 요즘 비즈니스 구어에서 매우 자주 쓴다.
examples: Instead of hiding that we're a small team, we leaned into it.
When the interview went off script, I leaned into the conversation.
She leaned into the awkward silence and asked a bolder question.

similar.example: We embraced the change instead of fighting it.
They doubled down on the original plan.

expressions.quote: fall flat with audiences of color
expressions.nuance_ko: 농담, 발표, 제품이 반응을 얻지 못할 때 쓴다. 'fall flat with + 청중'으로 대상을 붙인다. 'fail'보다 부드럽고 구어적이다.
examples: My joke fell flat in the meeting. Nobody laughed.
The new menu fell flat with the lunch crowd.
The ad campaign fell flat with younger customers.

similar.example: The joke just didn't land.
My presentation bombed.

expressions.nuance_ko: 금융에서 온 말이지만 일상 협상에서도 쓴다. 결과가 나빠도 버틸 수 있는 안전장치를 뜻한다. 'safety net'보다 전문적인 어감이다.
examples: A refund clause gives us downside protection if the event gets cancelled.
I took a part-time job as downside protection while launching my business.
Travel insurance is basically downside protection for your trip.

similar.example: Savings are my safety net.
We hired a backup to hedge against delays.

expressions.quote: it really cut into our business
expressions.nuance_ko: 'cut into profits/margins/sales'로 자주 쓴다. 경쟁이나 비용이 이익을 갉아먹는다는 뜻이다. 시간에도 쓴다(cut into my weekend).
examples: Cheap online options have cut into our store's sales.
Rising rent is cutting into our margins.
Work emails keep cutting into my weekends.

similar.example: Fees eat into your returns.
Discounts eroded our margins.

expressions.quote: we sort of pivoted toward documentaries
expressions.nuance_ko: 스타트업식 표현이지만 지금은 일반 업무 대화에서도 쓴다. 필요에 의해 전략을 바꿨다는 뉘앙스다. 'pivot to/toward'를 쓴다.
examples: After the layoffs, the company pivoted toward subscription services.
I pivoted toward data work when the old role disappeared.
When it rained, we pivoted toward indoor activities.

similar.example: We shifted focus to smaller clients.
The airline changed course after complaints.

expressions.quote: keep tabs on the competition at Sundance
expressions.nuance_ko: 감시라기보다 상황을 계속 확인한다는 느낌이다. 경쟁사나 가족 모두에 쓴다. 'keep an eye on'과 비슷하지만 정보 파악에 더 가깝다.
examples: I keep tabs on what our competitors are charging.
She keeps tabs on her parents by calling every Sunday.
Can you keep tabs on the flight status for me?

similar.example: Keep an eye on the luggage.
I stay on top of the news every morning.

expressions.quote: basically boils down to good old-fashioned spycraft
expressions.nuance_ko: 복잡한 상황의 핵심을 짚는 말이다. 토론에서 'It all boils down to…'로 결론을 압축할 때 유용하다.
examples: It all boils down to trust, doesn't it?
The decision basically boils down to price versus quality.
Most disagreements at work boil down to unclear expectations.

similar.example: It comes down to timing.
The bottom line is we need more time.

expressions.quote: it could have gone either way
expressions.meaning_ko: 어느 쪽으로든 결과가 날 수 있었다
expressions.nuance_ko: 결과가 아슬아슬했다고 돌아볼 때 쓴다. 시제는 'could have gone'이다. 아직 진행 중이면 'could go either way'.
examples: The vote was close. It could have gone either way.
The interview could have gone either way, honestly.
The match could go either way until the last set.

The org chart is in flux after the reorganization.
The housing market has been in flux all year.

warmup.q: When you scroll through streaming options, how do you decide what to watch? Does hype or word of mouth matter to you?
warmup.hint_ko: 추천 알고리즘, 리뷰, 지인 추천, 예고편 등 자신의 선택 기준을 구체적 사례로 설명.

warmup.q: Have you ever been to a festival, conference or event where deals or connections happened informally, like at a party?
warmup.hint_ko: 비공식 자리에서 오간 대화나 인맥 경험, 또는 그런 장면을 상상해서 이야기.

opinion.q: John says overhyped films often fail, so the best instinct is to downplay them. Do you agree that managing expectations downward is the smarter strategy?
opinion.hint_ko: 기대치 관리의 장단점, 직장 발표나 제품 출시 사례, 과소 약속 후 과잉 이행 전략과 연결.

opinion.q: The episode shows that a few decision-makers decide which films reach the world. How concerned should we be about that concentration of taste?
opinion.hint_ko: 게이트키핑, 다양성, 알고리즘과 대형 플랫폼의 영향, 다른 산업의 유사 사례를 예로.

debate.q: Is the 'Sundance theater' of stunts, secret screenings and exclusive parties a legitimate part of the art market, or does it distort which films succeed?
debate.for: 주목 경제에서 스토리텔링과 희소성은 정당한 마케팅이며, 좋은 영화가 눈에 띄도록 돕는다.
debate.against: 작품의 질보다 이벤트와 인맥이 성패를 좌우해 불공정하고 자원이 있는 쪽만 유리해진다.

debate.q: Should a filmmaker pick the distributor offering the most money or the one offering the best long-term partnership?
debate.for: 최고가를 택해야 한다. 제작비 회수와 재정적 안정이 다음 작품을 보장하기 때문이다.
debate.against: 장기 관계, 배급 규모, 시상 캠페인 지원이 단기 금액보다 커리어 가치가 크다.

roleplay.scenario: You are a sales agent at a film festival. A streaming company's buyer loved your documentary, but needs a boss's approval before making an offer. You must set up the next step and negotiate the terms.
roleplay.your_role: Sales agent representing an independent documentary
roleplay.partner_role: Buyer from a streaming platform who is interested but cautious about budget
goals: Arrange a private screening for the decision-maker, using phrases like 'could have gone either way' or 'make ourselves scarce'.
Make the case for the film's audience and offer some 'downside protection', such as test-screening results.
Push back on the price and commitment while keeping the relationship warm, with 'it comes down to…' or 'lean into…'.

useful_phrases.phrase: The details are still in flux.
It could have gone either way.

shadowing.reason_ko: '~해야 하고, 그러고 나서 ~해야 한다'는 대조 구조와 'Jekyll and Hyde' 비유로 협상 태도를 설명하는 리듬이 좋다.
'The roads of … are littered with…'와 'it may seem counterintuitive, but…'로 반직관적 주장을 펼치는 전형적인 논증 패턴이다.
'lean into your luck'과 'pivot'으로 전체 교훈을 간결하게 압축하는 마무리 문장이다.

difficulty.note_ko: 진행자의 말은 또렷한 내레이션이지만 업계 용어와 비유가 많다. 존 슬로스의 구어는 속도가 빠르고 끊김과 자기 수정이 잦으며, 영화 제목과 고유명사도 많이 나온다.

translations_sent.1-1: 며칠 전 밤에 소파에 앉아서 다들 그러듯이 스트리밍 영화 목록을 쭉 넘겨 보고 있었어요. 새로 나온 인디 코미디를 볼지, 묵직한 다큐멘터리를 볼지 고민하면서요.
translations_sent.2-2: 그러다 제가 실제로 볼 수 있는 선택지에 대해 생각하기 시작했어요. 얼마 전에 그 메뉴 뒤에 숨은 시장을 살짝 엿봤거든요. 어떤 영화가 여러분 근처 스크린에 걸리는지를 결정하는 협상과 전략 말이에요.
translations_sent.3-3: 그리고 영화 한 편이 무명에서 뽑혀 나오는 과정이 영화 못지않게 재미있을 수 있다는 걸 알게 됐어요.
translations_sent.4-4: 모든 건 어느 춥지만 화창한 1월 아침, 유타주 파크시티의 한 영화관 주차장에서 시작됐어요.
translations_sent.5-5: 2026 선댄스 영화제가 시작되기 직전에 도착해서 존 슬로스라는 분을 만났어요.
translations_sent.6-6: 혹시 누가 당신을 '미스터 선댄스'라고 부른 적 있나요?
translations_sent.8-8: 네, 2006년에 뉴욕 타임스 1면에 나왔던 것 같아요.
translations_sent.9-9: 그 기사에서 저를 선댄스의 왕이라고 불렀던 걸로 기억해요.
translations_sent.14-14: 요즘엔 그런 것에 반대하는 행진까지 있잖아요.
translations_sent.16-16: 존은 시네틱 미디어라는 회사의 설립자예요. 이 회사는 자금 조달부터 홍보까지 독립영화 세계의 온갖 일을 하죠.
translations_sent.17-17: 하지만 존이 가장 유명한 건 영화 세일즈 에이전트로서의 일이에요.
translations_sent.18-18: 존의 일은 독특한 영화 예술 작품을 팔 수 있는 상품으로 바꾸는 거예요.
translations_sent.19-19: 앞으로 일주일 정도 동안 그의 임무는 엔터테인먼트 업계 대형 회사들을 대표하는 소수의 바이어들이 자기 라인업의 영화를 보게 하고, 수백만 달러짜리 베팅을 연이어 하도록 설득하는 거예요.
translations_sent.20-20: 이 일에서 존의 파트너, 말하자면 왕의 오른팔은 그의 조카인 에릭 슬로스예요.
translations_sent.21-21: 우리 셋은 영화제 첫 상영을 기다리며 줄 선 엄청난 인파 앞에 서 있어요.
translations_sent.22-22: 등반을 다룬 다큐멘터리 '더 라스트 퍼스트, 윈터 K2'예요.
translations_sent.23-23: 하지만 에릭은 아주 특정한 몇 사람을 찾느라 눈을 크게 뜨고 있어요.
translations_sent.24-24: 이 영화제에서 우리 목적상 진짜 관객은 아주 적어요. 우리가 원하는 수준으로 다큐멘터리를 살 수 있는 사람이 한 열 명쯤이죠.
translations_sent.26-26: 영화제가 열리기 전에 가슴이 두근거리거나 하나요?
translations_sent.27-27: 네, 큰 경기 직전 몇 분 같은 느낌이에요.
translations_sent.28-28: 엔터테인먼트 업계에 남은 유일한 서부 개척지 같은 환경이고, 그래서 본질적으로 짜릿해요.
translations_sent.29-29: 존과 에릭의 일에서 큰 부분은 자기네 영화가 가능한 한 최고의 시간대와 장소에서 상영되도록 밀어붙이는 거예요.
translations_sent.30-30: 이 다큐멘터리의 경우, 파크시티에서 가장 큰 스크린과 좋은 음향 시스템을 갖춘 극장 중 하나를 잡는 데 성공했어요. 웅장한 야외 영화에 딱이죠.
translations_sent.31-31: 하지만 영화제 전체의 첫 상영 시간대를 받은 건 다소 운이 나쁜 편이었다고 에릭은 말해요.
translations_sent.32-32: 영화제 첫 상영이라서 사람들이 아직 도시에 도착하지 않았을까 봐 정말 초조했어요.
translations_sent.33-33: 지금 주위를 둘러보면서 보고 싶었던 사람들이 와 있는지 재차 확인하고 계신 거예요?
translations_sent.34-34: 바이어들이 들어오는 걸 계속 확인하고 있어요.
translations_sent.37-37: 사실 저희가 만든 트레이딩 카드도 있어요.
translations_sent.41-41: 애플, 아마존, 디즈니 쪽 사람들도 왔었고요.
translations_sent.42-42: 바로 그때 존이 희끗희끗한 머리에 두꺼운 검은 테 안경을 쓴 남자에게 손을 흔듭니다.
translations_sent.47-47: 유진 에르난데스는 선댄스 영화제의 총괄 책임자입니다.
translations_sent.48-48: 해마다 그와 팀원들은 수천 편의 출품작을 100편 안팎으로 추려냅니다.
translations_sent.49-49: 하지만 영화제에 입성했다고 해서 영화가 실제로 팔린다는 보장은 없습니다.
translations_sent.52-52: 시장이 어떻게 반응할지 정확히 예측하기는 항상 어렵죠.
translations_sent.55-55: 저기 소니 클래식스의 인수 담당 책임자가 있네요.
translations_sent.57-57: 그러니까, 딜런이 수표를 써야 하고, 그러면 영화가 세상에 나가는 거죠.
translations_sent.58-58: 이 순간 전까지는 엔터테인먼트 업계가 이렇게 작고 개인적인 세계일 수 있다는 걸 제대로 몰랐던 것 같아요. 한 영화의 상업적 운명이 결국 소수의 의사결정자들의 취향과 계산에 달려 있을 수 있다는 사실 말이에요.
translations_sent.60-60: 가운데 쪽에 자리가 많이 남아 있으니 최대한 가운데로 앉아 주세요. 감사합니다.
translations_sent.61-61: 우리는 극장 앞쪽 근처에 자리를 잡습니다.
translations_sent.62-62: 객석 조명이 어두워지고 관객들이 조용해지며, 영화제의 첫 빛이 스크린을 밝힙니다.
translations_sent.63-63: 존과 에릭은 극장 안을 슬쩍슬쩍 둘러봅니다. 이 첫 관객들의 반응에 따라 밤새 이어지는 입찰 전쟁이 벌어질 수도, 선댄스 역사의 휴지통으로 사라질 수도 있기 때문이죠.
translations_sent.66-66: 독립영화 세계에서 선댄스 같은 곳에 작품을 올리는 건 영화 제작이라는 산의 정상에 오르는 것처럼 보일 수 있습니다.
translations_sent.67-67: 하지만 적어도 상업적인 면에서 보면, 영화제에 선정되는 건 베이스캠프에 도착하는 것에 더 가깝습니다.
translations_sent.68-68: 극장과 스트리밍 플랫폼이라는 정상에 오르려면, 그 영화를 전 세계 스크린에 올려줄 수 있는 누군가에게 실제로 팔아야 하거든요.
translations_sent.70-70: 노련한 세일즈 에이전트 두 사람을 따라 선댄스를 누빕니다. 초대받은 사람만 가는 파티, 화제를 노린 퍼포먼스, 기업 스파이 작전, 은밀한 뒷거래라는 관문을 통과하면서요.
translations_sent.71-71: 이 영화제가 업계를 어떻게 바꿔놓았는지 알아보고, 영화라는 예술을 차가운 현금으로 바꾸는 복잡한 비즈니스를 슬쩍 들여다봅니다.
translations_sent.72-72: 영화가 전 세계 스크린에 오르는 경로는 여러 가지입니다.
translations_sent.73-73: 우선 할리우드 스튜디오가 만드는 마블이나 픽사 영화 같은 대형 블록버스터가 있죠.
translations_sent.74-74: 넷플릭스가 자사 플랫폼에서 스트리밍하려고 만든 영화 같은 것들도 있고요.
translations_sent.75-75: 그리고 우리가 독립영화라고 부르는, 더 패기 있고 예산이 적은 영화들이 있습니다. 이런 영화들은 오스카 시상식 무대에 오르기도 하죠.
translations_sent.76-76: 이런 영화들은 대부분 선댄스 같은 영화제에서 사고팔립니다.
translations_sent.77-77: '선댄스의 왕'이라고도 불리는 세일즈 에이전트 존 슬로스는 1980년대 중반에 처음 이 영화제에 가기 시작했습니다.
translations_sent.78-78: 영화 스타 로버트 레드퍼드가 독립영화 제작을 기리고 할리우드의 시장 논리로부터 지키기 위한 장소로 세운 영화제였죠.
translations_sent.79-79: 하지만 존은 특히 한 영화의 대성공이 업계가 이 영화제를 바라보는 시각을 순식간에 바꿔놓았다고 말합니다.
translations_sent.80-80: 선댄스의 변곡점은 1989년이었어요. 소더버그가 「섹스, 거짓말, 그리고 비디오테이프」를 들고 왔을 때죠.
translations_sent.82-82: 스티븐 소더버그의 「섹스, 거짓말, 그리고 비디오테이프」는 저예산 장편영화였는데, 영화제를 완전히 휩쓸었고 결국 3,600만 달러가 넘는 수익을 올렸어요.
translations_sent.83-83: 그리고 존 말로는 그런 수익률이 할리우드 업계 전체에 독립 예술영화도 스튜디오 블록버스터와 경쟁할 수 있다는 걸 보여줬대요.
translations_sent.84-84: 그 후로 할리우드 스튜디오들은 독립영화를 사들이고 제작하는 전문 부서를 자체적으로 열기 시작했어요.
translations_sent.85-85: 그리고 선댄스는 그 새로운 독립영화들의 가장 큰 시장 중 하나가 됐죠. 영화배우, 떠오르는 감독, 기업 바이어, 그리고 존 같은 세일즈 에이전트들로 북적였어요.
translations_sent.86-86: 존의 말로는 독립영화를 실제로 파는 기술은 일종의 섬세한 투스텝 춤이라고 생각하면 된대요. 처음에는 할리우드의 실력자가 될 만한 사람들이 가능한 한 가장 좋은 상영 환경에서 영화를 보게 만드는 게 제일 중요하거든요.
translations_sent.87-87: 하지만 세부 조건을 실제로 두들겨 맞추기 시작하는 두 번째 단계에서는 강경한 협상이 필요할 수 있어요.
translations_sent.88-88: 이건 늘 본질적인 갈등이었어요. 영화를 상영하기 전에는 배급사들이 우리 영화를 보러 오게 하려면 비위를 맞춰야 하니까요.
translations_sent.89-89: 그러다 일단 오고 나면 독한 사람으로 돌변해서 계약을 최대한 유리하게 만들어야 하죠.
translations_sent.91-91: 그러니까 지킬 박사와 하이드 같은 상황이에요.
translations_sent.92-92: 존은 회사 안에서 이런 긴장을 다루는 방법으로 일종의 감정 노동 분담을 해왔다고 해요.
translations_sent.93-93: 저는 항상 나쁜 경찰 역할이 더 편해요.
translations_sent.95-95: 그리고 배급사들이 영화를 보러 오게 하려고 붙임성 좋은 사람들을 항상 앞에 내세우려고 해요. 그래야 제가 갑자기 태도를 바꿔도 그렇게 이상해 보이지 않으니까요.
translations_sent.97-97: 하지만 그런 전환이 큰 부분을 차지해요.
translations_sent.98-98: 그런데 잠재적 구매자들과 탱고를 추는 방식은 팔려는 영화의 종류에 따라 달라요.
translations_sent.99-99: 저는 존에게 선댄스에서 40년 동안 성사시킨 가장 큰 계약들과 거기서 배운 점을 이야기해 달라고 부탁했어요.
translations_sent.100-100: 먼저 존은 이렇게 말했어요. 영화를 파는 게 일이니 최대한 크게 떠들어서 홍보해야 할 것 같지만, 화제를 너무 많이 만들면 진짜 위험이 있다고요.
translations_sent.101-101: 과거 선댄스의 길목에는 과대 홍보됐던 영화들의 시체가 널려 있어요.
translations_sent.102-102: 선댄스에 들어올 때 핫한 영화가 나갈 때도 핫한 영화인 경우는 절대 없어요.
translations_sent.103-103: 그래서 성공할 수 있다고 생각하는 영화가 있다면, 직관에 반하는 것 같지만 최선의 본능은 오히려 기대를 낮추는 거예요. 필요한 사람들은 모두 극장에 오게 하면서도 기대치는 최대한 낮게 만드는 거죠.
translations_sent.104-104: 존은 이 전략의 가장 좋은 사례 중 하나가 2003년에 있었다고 해요.
translations_sent.105-105: 그의 회사 시네틱은 영화제를 앞두고 처음 영화를 만든 몇몇 감독들의 저예산 독립 장편영화를 접하게 됐어요.
translations_sent.106-106: 그건 말하자면 갑자기 불쑥 들어온 영화였어요.
translations_sent.107-107: 20만 달러짜리 영화였는데, 아이다호주 프레스턴에 사는 모르몬교 청년들이 만든 거였어요.
translations_sent.109-109: 존과 동료들은 다음 선댄스를 위해 그 감독들을 자신들의 세일즈 라인업에 넣기로 계약했어요. 하지만 이번에는 그 사실을 비밀로 하는 게 최선의 전략이라고 판단했대요.
translations_sent.110-110: 관객들이 자기들만큼 이 영화를 매력적으로 느낄 거라고, 그리고 이 숨은 보석에 대해 사람들이 입소문을 내며 자연스럽게 생기는 기세가 바이어들에게 직접 홍보하는 것보다 판매 가능성을 더 높여줄 거라고 내기를 건 거예요.
translations_sent.118-118: 사자랑 호랑이를 섞은 거야. 능력이랑 마법을 위해 교배된 거지.
translations_sent.119-119: 「나폴레옹 다이너마이트」의 발견은 그 영화제 안에서 폭탄급이었어요.
translations_sent.121-121: 바로 그때 시장이 정말, 뭐랄까, 성숙해졌죠.
translations_sent.124-124: 그리고 존은 이 영화가 개봉한 뒤에 벌어진 일을 보면 왜 스튜디오와 배급사들이 인디 영화에 그렇게 관심을 가졌는지 알 수 있다고 말해요.
translations_sent.125-125: 극장 수익이 4,400만 달러였는데, DVD 판매까지 합치면 수익이 제 기억엔 1억 7,000만 달러쯤 됐어요. 20만 달러짜리 영화가요.
translations_sent.126-126: 그런데 보통은, 존의 말로는, 세일즈 에이전트의 일이란 기본적으로 바이어를 쫓아다니면서 수요를 끌어내는 거라고 해요.
translations_sent.127-127: 하지만 거기에도 예외가 있다고 그는 말해요.
translations_sent.128-128: 운 좋게 인기 있는 영화를 갖게 되면, 제 생각엔 그때 상황이 뒤집히는 거예요.
translations_sent.129-129: 더 이상 우리가 파는 쪽이 아니게 되는 거죠.
translations_sent.130-130: 이제는 배급사가 감독과 제작진을 설득해야 해요. 18개월 동안 낳아 기른 자식 같은 작품을, 그 작품과 아무 상관 없던 사람에게, 게다가 그 뒤에 개봉할 다른 영화가 열 편이나 있는 사람에게 왜 맡겨야 하는지를요.
translations_sent.131-131: 존은 「나폴레옹 다이너마이트」 몇 년 뒤에 나온 영화 한 편을 대표적인 사례로 꼽아요.
translations_sent.132-132: 엉뚱한 가족 로드트립 영화, 「리틀 미스 선샤인」이었죠.
translations_sent.134-134: 자, 리틀 미스 선샤인은 앨버커키에 사는 모든 아이들을 위한 미인 대회인데, 여섯 살이나 일곱 살이어야 하고 여자애여야 해.
translations_sent.135-135: 지난달에 올리브가 여기 왔을 때 기억나? 지역 리틀 미스 선샤인에서 준우승했잖아.
translations_sent.136-137: 이제 주 대회에 나갈 자격이 생겼어, 레돈도에서-- [환호성]
translations_sent.138-138: 존과 동료들은 관객을 사로잡을 만한 영화를 손에 넣었다고 생각했고, 그래서 눈에 안 띄게 가려고 하기보다 약간 화제몰이를 하기로 했어요.
translations_sent.139-139: 그들은 선댄스 프로그래머들을 설득해서 영화제 첫 금요일 밤, 마을에서 가장 크고 웅장한 극장에 시사회를 잡았어요.
translations_sent.140-140: 사실 고등학교 강당이긴 한데, 이상하게 영화를 상영하기에 분위기가 뜨거운 곳이라서 영화가 잘 먹히는 곳이거든요.
translations_sent.141-141: 그래도 조명이 어두워질 때, 존 말로는 이 영화가 실제 관객에게 어떻게 받아들여질지 아무도 정말 몰랐대요.
translations_sent.144-144: 마치 극장에 아산화질소를 흘려보낸 것 같았죠.
translations_sent.145-145: 그리고 영화가 한 15분쯤 지났을 때 제 어시스턴트한테 말했어요, 여기서 나가야 해, 안 그러면 우린 죽는다고.
translations_sent.146-146: 이게, 그러니까 불이 켜지면 사람들이 우리한테 몰려들 테니까요.
translations_sent.147-147: 존은 이게 분명 꿈같은 시나리오였지만 그래도 제대로 대처해야 한다는 걸 알았다고 말해요.
translations_sent.148-148: 그래서 상영 도중에 그는 영화 제작진에게 속삭였어요.
translations_sent.149-149: 제가 말했죠, 자, 파티가 열리는 곳으로 가세요, 전 사라질 테니까요.
translations_sent.150-150: 존과 그의 어시스턴트는 전략적으로 극장을 빠져나갔어요.
translations_sent.151-151: 어시스턴트랑 저는 옆문으로 나갔는데, 주차장으로 가는 줄 알았거든요.
translations_sent.152-152: 그런데 결국 고등학교 미식축구장 한가운데로 나왔어요. 눈이 60센티미터는 쌓여 있었죠.
translations_sent.154-154: 제 어시스턴트는 손까지 베였고요, 아주 난리였죠.
translations_sent.156-156: 고속도로로 나가서 루비 튜즈데이라는 곳에 갔어요. 샐러드 바 무한 리필로 유명한 곳이죠.
translations_sent.158-158: 제 전화기는 완전히 폭발했는데 전화는 단 한 통도 받지 않았어요.
translations_sent.159-159: 그리고 제작진에게 말해뒀죠, 바이어들이 미쳐 날뛰면서 저를 찾아 파티에 오면 그냥 이렇게 말하라고요, 슬로스가 어디 있는지 모르겠다고.
translations_sent.160-160: 자기 할 일 하러 간 것 같다고요.
translations_sent.162-162: 네, 그렇게 한 세 시간쯤 했죠.
translations_sent.163-163: 그러고 나서 바이어들을 우선순위에 두고 한 팀씩 찾아오게 하기로 했어요.
translations_sent.164-164: 그러니까 매년 존과 시네틱의 동료들은 마을 바로 외곽에 있는 같은 통나무 샬레를 빌려요.
translations_sent.165-165: 바로 거기가 존과 그의 팀, 그리고 '리틀 미스 선샤인'의 감독들이 모여서 다음 절차, 다들 탐내는 입찰 전쟁을 시작하는 곳이에요.
translations_sent.166-166: 관심 있는 바이어들이 저마다 최고의 프레젠테이션을 준비해 오는 때죠.
translations_sent.167-167: 그런데 이건 단순히 돈을 제일 많이 제시하는 문제가 아니에요.
translations_sent.168-168: 바이어들은 저마다 자기들이 이 영화를 더 넓은 세상에 내놓기에 가장 좋은 위치에 있다고 제작진과 에이전트들을 설득하고 싶어 해요.
translations_sent.169-169: 자기들이 해 온 비슷한 영화들을 얘기하죠.
translations_sent.170-170: 얼마나 투자하고 얼마나 힘을 쏟을지도 얘기하고요.
translations_sent.171-171: 이렇게 묻는 거죠. 극장을 몇 곳이나 보장하시겠어요?
translations_sent.173-173: 존은 어떤 제작진은 아카데미 시상식 캠페인에 돈을 충분히 쓰겠다고 약속하는 회사를 더 선호할 수도 있다고 해요.
translations_sent.174-174: 사회 문제를 다룬 영화라면, 특정 지역사회에서 상영되는 것이나 영화가 더 폭넓은 정책 논의를 불러일으키는 것을 가장 중요하게 생각할 수도 있고요.
translations_sent.175-175: 하지만 신인 감독이라면 올바른 배급사를 고르는 일은 상당 부분 장기전과도 관련이 있어요, 왜냐하면요.
translations_sent.176-176: 선택한 회사가 그 감독이 이 영화 이후에도 계속 함께 일하게 될 회사일 가능성이 크거든요.
translations_sent.180-180: '리틀 미스 선샤인'의 경우, 존의 말로는 제작진이 결국 한 회사의 계획에 마음이 움직였대요. 아트하우스 극장가를 훨씬 넘어서 상영하고, 시상식 캠페인을 지원하고, 1,000만 달러가 넘는 금액을 지불하겠다는 계획이었죠.
translations_sent.181-181: 그 영화는 밤을 꼬박 새우고 아침에 당시 기준 기록적인 금액으로 계약을 마무리한 작품이었어요.
translations_sent.182-182: 이렇게 거의 만장일치로 호평받은 영화가 판매라는 관문을 통과하게 되는 거예요.
translations_sent.184-184: 존은 영화를 파는 데 전략과 노동과 운이 얼마나 들어가는지, 그리고 그걸 더 많은 관객에게 전하는 일이 어떤지 제대로 이해하고 싶다면 영화 '프레셔스'의 이야기보다 더 좋은 예는 아마 없을 거라고 해요.
translations_sent.185-185: 꽤 강렬한 영화예요. 과체중의 흑인 소녀가 모두에게 학대만 당하는 이야기거든요.
translations_sent.191-191: 존은 2009년 1월 선댄스 영화제를 앞두고 '프레셔스'에 대해 처음 들었다고 해요.
translations_sent.192-192: 리 대니얼스라는 비교적 경험이 적은 감독에게서였죠.
translations_sent.195-195: 하지만 스스로에게 물어봐야 해요. 이 영화의 관객은 누굴까?
translations_sent.196-196: 영화를 팔 때 하는 일 중 하나가 배급사에게 관객이 누구고 얼마나 큰지 설득하는 거니까요.
translations_sent.197-197: 존은 리에게 영화가 아름답다고, 판매를 돕고 싶다고 말하지만, 신체적·성적 학대라는 주제 때문에 팔기 어려울 수 있다고 걱정해요.
translations_sent.198-198: 그래서 리 대니얼스에게 말했죠. 전에 이런 영화에 관여한 적이 있다고요.
translations_sent.199-199: '슬램'이라는 영화를 했는데, 선댄스에서 큰 화제였고 라이온스게이트에 팔았어요.
translations_sent.200-200: 그러고 나서 컴턴 일대의 매직 존슨 극장에 영화를 곧바로 가져가서 흑인 관객 대상으로 시사회를 했는데, 반응이 정말 처참했어요.
translations_sent.201-201: 존은 '슬램'이 바이어들에게 일종의 교훈적인 사례였다고 해요.
translations_sent.202-202: 그건 어떤 영화는 선댄스의 대체로 백인이고 비교적 부유한 관객들에게는 히트를 쳐도, 유색인종 관객에게는 반응이 시들하거나 그 반대일 수도 있다는 걸 보여줬어요.
translations_sent.203-203: 때로는 영화가 그 모든 관객층 사이의 어딘가 어정쩡한 불쾌한 골짜기에 빠지기도 하고요.
translations_sent.204-204: 그리고 존은 「프레셔스」가 바로 그런 위험에 처할 수 있다고 걱정했죠.
translations_sent.205-205: 그런데 리 대니얼스는, 이건 칭찬할 만한 부분인데, 당신이 틀렸다고 말했어요.
translations_sent.207-207: 할렘 125번가에 있는 매직 존슨 극장에서 시사회를 잡겠다고요.
translations_sent.208-208: 그 객석에 있는 사람은 전부 유색인종일 거라고요.
translations_sent.209-209: 와서 객석에 앉아 보면, 이 영화가 선댄스 관객 앞에서 상영될 때와 흑인 관객 앞에서 상영될 때 완전히 다르게 먹힌다는 걸 보게 될 거라고요.
translations_sent.211-211: 그래서 우리는 시사회를 했어요. 점수 같은 걸 매기는 거요, 그것도 쓸 수 있는 도구니까요.
translations_sent.212-212: 영화가 상영됐는데, 사람들이 웃다가 의자에서 굴러떨어질 지경이었어요.
translations_sent.214-214: 그래서 우리는 그 시사회 결과를 들고 선댄스에 갔어요. 배급사들이 영화는 마음에 들지만 백인 관객이 안 볼지, 흑인 관객이 안 볼지 모르겠다고 하면, 흑인 관객이 이 영화를 아주 좋아할 거라는 테스트 결과를 보여줄 수 있게요.
translations_sent.215: 그게 일종의 손실 방어책이 되는 거였죠.
translations_sent.216-216: 그래서 존은 영화제에서 이 영화의 판매 대행을 맡기로 해요.
translations_sent.217-217: 그들은 영화를 선댄스에 가져가서, 큰손 바이어들이 상영관에 와서 보게 하려고 할 수 있는 건 다 했어요.
translations_sent.218-218: 그 큰 극장에서 영화를 상영했는데, 하비 와인스타인이 저한테 와서 이러는 거예요. 훌륭한 영화인데 어떻게 마케팅해야 할지 모르겠다고요.
translations_sent.220-220: 그런데 존 말로는 타일러 페리와 연줄이 있는 누군가가 이 영화를 아주 좋아했고, 가능한 한 빨리 타일러에게 보여줘야 한다고 했대요.
translations_sent.222-222: 타일러 페리가 오바마 취임식 때문에 워싱턴으로 가는 중이었다는 거예요.
translations_sent.223-223: 그래서 필름 프린트를 워싱턴 DC로 보냈어요.
translations_sent.224-224: 타일러 페리가 그걸 보고 완전히 뒤집어져서는, 제가 도울 수 있는 게 뭐가 있겠냐고 했어요.
translations_sent.225-225: 그리고 리 대니얼스는 워낙 약삭빠른 사람이라--
translations_sent.230-230: 하지만 선댄스 마지막 며칠이 되도록 존과 리는 오프라가 영화를 봤는지, 마음에 들어 했는지 아직 듣지 못했어요.
translations_sent.231-231: 영화제에서 영화는 그럭저럭 괜찮은 반응이었어요. 관객 반응은 대체로 따뜻했고 긍정적인 평도 몇 개 나왔죠. 하지만 실제 판매로 이어질 만한 구체적인 관심은 여전히 없었어요.
translations_sent.234-234: 우리가 시상식에 앉아 있는데 객석에서 리 대니얼스의 휴대폰이 울려요.
translations_sent.236-236: 그런데 어쩐 일인지 그는 그 전화를 받았어요.
translations_sent.238-238: 오프라가 말했죠. 당신 영화가 저를 완전히 무너뜨렸어요.
translations_sent.240-240: 그리고 이 영화는 선댄스에서 관객상과 심사위원대상을 둘 다 받게 돼요.
translations_sent.242-242: 존의 말로는 영화제가 끝난 뒤 그 영화를 라이언스게이트에 약 500만 달러에 팔았다고 해요.
translations_sent.243-243: 그리고 그 영화는 결국 5천만 달러 넘게 벌어들였죠.
translations_sent.244-244: 흑인 관객과 백인 관객 모두에게 사랑받았어요.
translations_sent.245-245: 하지만 이런 일련의 사건들이 일어나지 않았다면 그냥 묻혀 버렸을 수도 있었죠.
translations_sent.247-247: 그러니까, 행운에 올라타거나 예상하지 못한 상황을 알아차리고 방향을 틀어야 하는 거예요.
translations_sent.248-248: 존은 <프레셔스>의 이야기가 영화가 사고팔리는 방식이 얼마나 우연에 크게 좌우되는지, 그리고 영화제 무대에만 영원히 갇혀 있을 영화와 전국 극장으로 뻗어 나가는 영화를 가르는 놀라운 거래 성사 과정을 보여 주는 완벽한 사례라고 말해요.
translations_sent.249-249: 자, <프레셔스> 이후 몇 년 동안 영화 업계 자체도 꽤 큰 우여곡절을 겪었어요.
translations_sent.250-250: 이른바 스트리밍 전쟁 때는 판매자 우위 시장이었어요. 존 같은 세일즈 에이전트가 경쟁이 치열한 스트리밍 업체와 전통적인 영화 배급사를 맞붙여 더 좋은 조건을 끌어낼 수 있었죠. 그런데 코로나로 극장이 텅 비고 대형 합병이 잇따르면서 할리우드가 허리띠를 졸라매자 시장은 한풀 꺾였어요.
translations_sent.253-253: 자, 지금까지 선댄스의 과거를 대표하는 몇몇 대형 거래를 시간 여행하듯 살펴봤습니다.
translations_sent.254-254: 이제 올해 영화제로 돌아와서, 요즘 영화 구매자들의 마음을 움직이려면 어떤 일을 해야 하는지 가까이서 들여다볼게요.
translations_sent.255-255: 기억하시겠지만, 이야기는 영화제 첫 상영작에서 시작됐어요. 존과 에릭 슬로스가 판매하고 있는 등반 다큐멘터리 <The Last First, Winter K2>였죠.
translations_sent.256-256: 상영이 끝나고 저는 에릭을 만나 앞으로 일주일이 어떻게 흘러갈지 들어 봤어요.
translations_sent.257-257: 다음 한 주는 폭발적으로 바쁜 순간들 사이사이에 긴 기다림이 끼어 있는 시간이에요.
translations_sent.258-258: 어떤 부분은 약간 연옥 같은 느낌도 있고요.
translations_sent.260-260: 네, 가만히 앉아서 사람들이 전화해 주기를 기다리는 시간이 정말 많아요.
translations_sent.261-261: 에릭은 영화제 개막이 앞으로 닷새쯤 이어질 경주의 출발 신호총 같다고 말해요.
translations_sent.262-262: 그런데 존의 설명으로는 성패를 가르는 전략과 경쟁의 상당 부분이 사실 영화제 훨씬 전에 시작돼요. 영화를 홍보하고 구매자의 제안을 받는 일 외에도, 존의 일은 매년 보는 1,000편이 넘는 영화 중에서 가능성 있는 작품을 골라내고 감독들이 자기 회사에 영화 대행을 맡기도록 설득하는 거거든요.
translations_sent.263-263: 존은 최근 몇 년 사이 그 일이 훨씬 어려워졌다고 말해요. 시네틱은 이 시장의 초창기 주자 가운데 하나였는데, 지난 10~20년 사이 새로운 경쟁자들이 이들의 영역을 파고들고 있거든요.
translations_sent.264-264: 윌리엄 모리스 인데버나 크리에이티브 아티스츠 에이전시 같은 할리우드 대형 에이전시들은 배우, 작가, 감독을 대리하죠.
translations_sent.265-265: 이들은 여러 프로젝트가 시작될 수 있도록 이미 거래를 짜고 있었고, 그래서 존의 말로는 영화를 팔 때가 되면 그 협상도 자기들이 맡아야 한다고 점점 더 많이 제안하기 시작했대요.
translations_sent.266-266: 그래서 존과 에릭이 원래라면 판매 목록에 올렸을 영화 상당수가 이미 다른 곳에 넘어가 있었어요.
translations_sent.267-267: 그게 우리 사업을 정말 크게 갉아먹었어요. 그래서 수년 동안 극영화를 확보하기가 정말 힘들었던 이유 중 하나죠.
translations_sent.270-270: 우리도 살아남아야 하니까 다큐멘터리 쪽으로 방향을 틀었고, 시장에서 다큐멘터리의 가치를 높이려고 열심히 노력했어요.
translations_sent.271-271: 올해 선댄스에서 시네틱이 대행하는 영화 10편 중 여섯 편이 다큐멘터리예요.
translations_sent.272-272: 이게 영화제를 앞두고 존과 에릭이 맞닥뜨린 경쟁 상황이에요.
translations_sent.273-273: 하지만 막상 영화제에 도착하면 적합한 구매자를 자리에 앉히는 것뿐 아니라, 호의적인 관객으로 객석을 채우고, 영화 평론가나 화제성 있는 인플루언서를 몇 명 불러서 입소문에 불을 붙여 구매자들이 제안을 하도록 슬쩍 떠미는 것도 원해요.
translations_sent.274-274: 저는 이 전략을 '서사 통제하기', 말하자면 인셉션이라고 부르길 좋아해요.
translations_sent.275-275: 이건 늘 선댄스 판매 게임의 일부였지만, 존은 레터박스드나 X 같은 플랫폼 때문에 어떤 영화에 대한 논의가 누구에게나 열리면서 딱 맞는 때에 딱 맞는 평을 조합해 내기가 훨씬 어려워졌다고 말해요.
translations_sent.276-276: 맞아요, 그리고 영화에 대해 가장 먼저 글을 쓰는 사람이 여론을 좌우하는 목소리가 될 수 있어요.
translations_sent.277-277: 그리고 자기 영화를 둘러싼 서사를 통제하려는 것 말고도, 존과 에릭은 선댄스에서 경쟁 상황을 계속 살펴야 해요. 자기들이 대행하지 않는 모든 영화에 구매자들이 어떻게 반응하는지도 파악해야 하고요.
translations_sent.278-278: 그중 일부는 기본적으로 구식 첩보 활동에 가까워요.
translations_sent.280-280: 이 업계 커뮤니티에 완전히 연결돼 있죠.
translations_sent.281-281: 그냥 사람들을 내보내는 거예요. 일부는 상영회에 가서 끝나고 누가 모여 있는지 보고요.
translations_sent.283-283: 저는 이걸 "적도 아군도 아닌 프레너미 전선 너머"라고 부르고 싶은데요, 가끔 다른 회사 영화를 두고 입찰 경쟁이 벌어지면 존과 에릭의 판매 전망에 영향을 줄 수 있으니까요.
translations_sent.284-284: 이 영화제에 온 바이어들, 그러니까 대형 극장 배급사나 스트리밍 회사들은 새 작품을 사들이는 데 쓸 수 있는 현금이 한정돼 있어요.
translations_sent.285-285: 그래서 모두가 탐내는 반짝반짝 빛나는 신상 작품이 하나 나오면, 낙찰자가 가려질 때까지는 큰돈과 관심이 거기에 묶여 버릴 수 있어요. 그러고 나서야 차점자들이 풀려나서 다른 영화를 쫓을 수 있게 되죠.
translations_sent.286-286: 자, 이런 정보 관리와 정보 수집 말고도, 에릭 말로는 가끔 구식 쇼맨십에 기대기도 한대요.
translations_sent.287-287: 바이어들을 사로잡으려고 일종의 이벤트성 깜짝쇼를 벌이는 거죠.
translations_sent.288-288: 올해는 예를 들어, 시네틱 슬레이트의 다큐멘터리 중에 '더 디サイ플'이라는 영화가 있는데, 전 세계에 단 한 장뿐인, 비밀리에 녹음된 우탱 클랜 앨범에 관한 이야기예요.
translations_sent.290-290: 그리고 영화제가 시작되고 이틀쯤 지났을 때 거기서 그를 만났어요.
translations_sent.291-291: 저희는 지금 파크시티에서 계곡 아래쪽으로 내려와, 선댄스 영화제 이사회 의장의 별장에 와 있어요.
translations_sent.293-293: 우탱 클랜의 앨범 〈Once Upon a Time in Shaolin〉에서 다섯 곡을 처음으로 전곡 청취하려고 왔어요.
translations_sent.298-298: 이 장르에 속하는 사례로는 거리 예술가 뱅크시를 다룬 다큐멘터리 〈Exit Through the Gift Shop〉의 시사회가 있어요.
translations_sent.299-299: 그때는 파크시티 곳곳에 뱅크시의 새 작품 몇 점이 수수께끼처럼 나타난 일과 맞물렸고, 또 한번은 영향력 있는 평론가들과 영화제 관객들이 무슨 영화인지도 모른 채 자정 비밀 상영회에 초대됐다가, 조던 필의 〈Get Out〉 월드 프리미어를 보고 깜짝 놀라기도 했죠.
translations_sent.300-300: 올해의 깜짝 이벤트로, 에릭은 한 번도 공개된 적 없는 앨범의 독점 청취 파티가 잠재 바이어들의 FOMO를 자극할 거라는 데 걸었어요.
translations_sent.301-301: 그럼 제가 녹음하거나 앨범 일부를 따도 되겠죠?
translations_sent.303-303: 앨범이 시작되면 모두 휴대폰을 욘더 파우치에 넣어야 하고, 앨범이 다 끝날 때까지 잠겨 있을 거예요.
translations_sent.305-305: 유일한 목표는 사람들이 이 경험을 즐기는 거예요.
translations_sent.306-306: 파티 도중에 수표책부터 꺼낼 필요는 없는 거죠?
translations_sent.308-308: [웃음] 댄스 플로어에서 입찰 경쟁이 시작될 수도 있겠네요.
translations_sent.309-309: 테이블을 하나 마련해 둘 테니, 질서 있게 줄을 서시면 돼요.
translations_sent.311-311: 그 저택 문 너머에서 제가 뭘 들었는지 궁금하신 분들께는 이렇게만 말씀드릴게요. 세이렌의 섬을 지나갈 때 배의 돛대에 몸을 묶었던 오디세우스처럼, 인간의 언어로는 도저히 담아낼 수 없는 노래들이 있다는 거예요.
translations_sent.312-312: 어쨌든 그 후 며칠 동안은 존과 에릭이 여러 상영회와 파티 사이를 뛰어다니는 바람에, 저는 두 사람을 여기저기서 얼핏얼핏 보는 게 전부였어요.
translations_sent.313-313: 마침내 월요일 밤, 저는 이들의 판매 시련의 대미를 장식하는 자리, 영화제 첫 주말의 마무리를 기념하는 아주 인기 많은 시네틱 파티에 와 있어요.
translations_sent.314-314: 제가 도착했을 때는 영하 3도쯤 되는 추위 속에 수십 명, 아니 수십, 수십 명이 밖에 줄을 서 있었어요.
translations_sent.315-315: 어떤 사람들은 한 시간 넘게 기다리고 있었고요.
translations_sent.316-316: 안에서는 바의 사람이 빽빽하게 몰린 구역에서 에릭을 찾았어요.
translations_sent.317-317: 여기는 하이 웨스트 살롱인데, 아마 선댄스에서 가장 오래된 파티 중 하나일 거예요.
translations_sent.318-318: 다들 지칠 대로 지쳐서 한데 어울려 마음껏 놀게 되는 자리이면서, 동시에 수많은 거래가 성사되는 모임이기도 해요.
translations_sent.320-320: 방에 갇혀 있고 다들 취해 있으면, 이런 대화를 하기가 쉬워지거든요.
translations_sent.321-321: 영화들이 진짜로 팔리는 방식이 바로 이래요. 곡괭이 테마의 옛날식 광부 술집에서 올드패션드 한 잔 놓고 말이죠.
translations_sent.324-324: 아쉽게도 저는 이 파티에서 술은 안 마셔요.
translations_sent.326-326: 네, 혼자만 멀쩡한 것도 나쁘지 않죠.
translations_sent.327-327: 네. [웃음] 이걸 '입이 가벼워야 거래가 술술 풀린다'는 전략이라고 부르죠. 사실 그 흥청망청하는 분위기 속에서 성사되는 거래는 눈에 띄지 않았는데, 이틀 뒤에 에릭과 존한테서 전화가 와요. 자기들의 아지트, 그러니까 오랜 세월 수많은 판매 계약을 성사시킨 시네틱의 통나무집 저택으로 와서 같이 있자고요.
translations_sent.328-328: 이들은 스트립 몰 주차장에서 저를 태워 산속으로 쏜살같이 데려갑니다.
translations_sent.330-330: 우린 지금 디어 밸리에 있는 콘도에 와 있는데, 24~25년째 계속 빌려 온 곳이에요.
translations_sent.331-331: 선댄스 영화제 역사상 가장 크고 중요한 거래 중 몇몇이 지금 앉아 계신 바로 그 자리에서 성사됐어요.
translations_sent.334-334: 존은 세계 굴지의 스트리밍 업체와 스튜디오 대표들이 와서 영화를 따내려고 설득하는 자리를 방 안에서 가리킵니다.
translations_sent.335-335: 그분들이 들어와서 앉고, 영화 제작자들도 앉죠.
translations_sent.340-340: 그러고는 존이 영화제 첫 상영 이후에 무슨 일이 있었는지 들려주기 시작합니다.
translations_sent.341-341: 알고 보니 대형 스트리밍 업체 한 곳의 다큐멘터리 총괄이 존과 에릭에게 연락해서 관심이 있다고 했대요.
translations_sent.342-342: 하지만 예산도 빠듯하고 기업 관료주의도 심한 요즘 같은 때엔, 상사의 승인이 나기 전에는 협상을 시작할 수가 없었어요.
translations_sent.343-343: 그래서 존과 회사 사람들은 곧바로 움직여서 링컨 로그 샬레 지하 극장에 비공개 상영회를 마련했습니다.
translations_sent.345-345: 그리고 영화를 틀어 놓고 우리는 자리를 피해 줬죠.
translations_sent.346-346: 어느 쪽으로든 갈 수 있는 상황이었어요.
translations_sent.347-347: 다큐멘터리 총괄이 영화를 아주 좋아한다는 건 알았지만, 이분이 마음에 안 들어 했다면 제안은 아마 나오지 않았을 거예요.
translations_sent.350-350: 존이 말한 '제안이 구체화된다'는 게 무슨 뜻인지 물어보니, 그는 잠시 망설입니다.
translations_sent.351-351: 이게 언제 방송될지 모르겠지만, 내일 방송된다면 말씀드릴 수 없어요.
translations_sent.354-354: 아, 저희가 첫 작품 계약을 막 마무리했는데요, 「The Last First, K2 in Winter」예요.
translations_sent.361-361: 알렉시, 당신이 제일 먼저 듣는 거예요.
translations_sent.362-362: 좋아요, 그럼 이건 미래로 보내는 타임캡슐이네요. 축하드려요.
translations_sent.366-366: 존 말로는 나머지 판매 건은 아직 유동적이지만, 진행 상황은 계속 알려주겠대요.
translations_sent.367-367: 일단 지금은 시내 반대편에서 하는 상영회에 가려고 서둘러 나가야 해요.
translations_sent.368-368: 우린 극장에 딱 맞춰 도착했고, 작별 인사를 나눈 뒤 저는 그가 인파 속으로 사라지는 걸 지켜봅니다.
translations_sent.369-369: 아니나 다를까, 선댄스를 다녀온 지 아홉 달쯤 지난 지금, 전자레인지에 팝콘을 돌리고 소파에 푹 파묻혀서 TV로 최신 스트리밍 목록을 넘겨보다 보면, 애플에서 스트리밍 중인 등산 다큐멘터리 〈The Last First〉와 방금 넷플릭스에 공개된 우탱 클랜 다큐멘터리 〈The Disciple〉이 눈에 들어와요.
translations_sent.370-370: 그런데 이제는 그 영화들을 만드는 데 들어간 예술적 노고뿐 아니라, 그 영화들을 세상에 내놓은 거래 과정도 함께 생각하게 돼요.
translations_sent.371-371: 그리고 물론 저는 끝도 없이 계속 스크롤을 내립니다. 왜냐하면 뭘 볼지 실제로 고르는 일, 여러분, 그게 가장 오르기 힘든 정상이거든요.
translations_sent.372-372: 이번 Planet Money 에피소드는 Emma Peaslee가 제작하고, Jess Jiang이 편집했으며, Sierra Juarez가 팩트체크를, Annlie Huang이 엔지니어링을 맡았습니다.
translations_sent.373-373: Alex Goldmark는 Planet Money의 총괄 프로듀서입니다.
